items.prompt: What does "CDN" stand for?
choices: Centralized Data Node
Content Delivery Network
Cached Domain Name
Content Distribution Node
items.explanation: CDN = Content Delivery Network: a set of distributed servers that deliver content from locations close to the visitor.

items.prompt: In CDN terminology, what is the "origin"?
choices: Any nearby edge server
The visitor's own browser
The single "true" server that owns the original data
The DNS server that resolves the domain
items.explanation: The origin is the authoritative server — the one place the real, canonical data lives. Edge servers hold copies of it, not the source itself.

items.prompt: What is an "edge server" (or PoP) in a CDN?
choices: A backup origin used only during outages
A server near visitors that holds cached copies of content
The load balancer in front of the origin
A server that only handles DNS lookups
items.explanation: Edge servers (Points of Presence) are distributed geographically and hold cached copies, so nearby visitors don't have to reach the origin.

items.prompt: What is a CDN's "core trick," according to the unit?
choices: Compressing every response to save bandwidth
Caching — storing a copy of a response closer to the requester
Encrypting traffic between visitor and origin
Load-balancing requests across multiple origins
items.explanation: The core mechanism is caching: keeping a copy of a response near the requester so it doesn't need to be regenerated or re-fetched from scratch every time.

items.prompt: Why can't a single origin server in one data center serve the whole world equally well?
choices: It can, as long as it has a fast enough internet connection
Distance and request load are both physical constraints a single location can't escape
Origin servers are legally restricted to one continent
DNS prevents a single origin from answering global traffic
items.explanation: A single location can't be physically close to every visitor on Earth, and it has a hard ceiling on how many requests per second it can serve — a CDN addresses both constraints by distributing copies.

items.prompt: A visitor in Sydney requests a page from an origin in Virginia with no CDN in front of it. What does that round trip primarily cost?
choices: Nothing extra — the internet routes everything equally fast
Significant latency, because the request and response both have to physically cross a long distance
Only DNS lookup time, not the actual data transfer
It costs more money but not more time
items.explanation: Physical distance translates directly into round-trip latency — tens to hundreds of milliseconds depending on how far the bytes have to travel each way.

items.prompt: True or false: a CDN replaces the origin server entirely once it's set up.
choices: True — the origin can be shut down once a CDN is in place
False — the origin remains the source of truth; the CDN just reduces how often it's asked
True, but only for static assets
False, but only during the initial setup period
items.explanation: The origin stays the authoritative source of truth. The CDN doesn't replace it — it reduces how many requests ever reach it.

items.prompt: Which of these is a CDN edge server most analogous to?
choices: A photocopy kept nearby so you don't have to visit the one original document every time
A security guard that blocks unauthorized visitors
A translator that converts content into different languages
A backup generator that only activates during a power outage
items.explanation: An edge server holds a copy (like a photocopy) near the requester, so most requests never need to reach the one original (the origin).

items.prompt: A company's origin server is in Virginia. Without a CDN, why do visitors in Sydney and London experience slower page loads than visitors in Washington, D.C.?
choices: Sydney and London have slower internet infrastructure in general
Every request has to physically travel the full round-trip distance to Virginia and back
The origin intentionally throttles international traffic
DNS takes longer to resolve for non-US visitors
items.explanation: Latency is largely a function of physical distance — a visitor thousands of kilometers from the origin pays for that distance on every single request, regardless of the origin's own capacity.

items.prompt: A startup argues: "We don't need a CDN — we'll just add more origin servers in Virginia to handle load." What problem does this fail to solve that a CDN would?

It addresses load capacity but does nothing about the physical distance for visitors far from Virginia
More origin servers in one location automatically reduces latency worldwide
It solves both problems equally well, making a CDN redundant
items.explanation: Adding more servers in the same location can help with load (more capacity to answer requests) but does nothing about distance — a visitor in Sydney still has to send bytes across the same long physical path.

items.explanation: The origin remains the source of truth and can still answer every request directly — it would just be slower (no nearby copies) and under far more load (no layer absorbing requests first).

items.prompt: Put these three layers in the order a request actually checks them, closest to the visitor first.
choices: Origin server, CDN edge cache, browser cache
Browser cache, CDN edge cache, origin server
CDN edge cache, browser cache, origin server
They are always checked simultaneously, not in order
items.explanation: A request checks the browser cache first (on-device), then the nearby CDN edge cache, and only reaches the origin if both of those miss.

items.prompt: If the browser already has a fresh cached copy of a resource, what happens?
choices: The request still goes all the way to the origin to double-check
The request never leaves the visitor's device at all
The request goes only as far as the CDN edge, skipping the browser cache check
Browser caches are never consulted for any request
items.explanation: A fresh browser-cache hit means the resource is served directly from the device — the request doesn't travel over the network at all.

items.prompt: What does the CDN edge cache typically hold, compared to the browser cache?
choices: Only content unique to one specific visitor's device
Content shared across many visitors near that particular edge location
Nothing — edge caches never store actual response bodies
Exactly the same content as the origin, with no filtering
items.explanation: A browser cache holds what one visitor reuses across their own visits; a CDN edge cache holds content shared across many visitors near that PoP.

items.prompt: Why does "a request only travels as far as it has to" matter for the origin's workload?
choices: It doesn't — the origin sees every request regardless of caching
Every layer that successfully answers a request removes load from every layer behind it, including the origin
It only matters for reducing the visitor's own device battery usage
It matters only for requests that fail with an error
items.explanation: Each layer that can answer locally (browser cache, then edge cache) means one fewer request reaching the next layer — ultimately sparing the origin, the hardest layer to scale.

items.prompt: What is the origin server's role in the three-layer model?
choices: It's consulted first, before any cache, to guarantee freshness
It's the layer of last resort — asked only when both the browser and edge caches miss
It's bypassed entirely once a CDN is configured
It only serves requests during a cache invalidation
items.explanation: The origin is the authoritative source of truth, but it's only reached when neither the browser cache nor the CDN edge cache can answer the request.

items.prompt: A visitor requests a page, and their browser cache is empty (first visit ever). Which layer does the request reach next?
choices: It skips straight to the origin, bypassing the CDN
The nearest CDN edge cache, which may already have a copy from other visitors
A randomly selected edge server anywhere in the world
It waits for the browser cache to be manually populated first
items.explanation: A browser-cache miss sends the request to the nearest edge server next — which may well already hold a cached copy from other nearby visitors, even if this is this visitor's first request.

items.prompt: When a response travels back from the origin through the CDN edge to the browser, what typically happens at each layer along the way?
choices: Nothing — only the browser is allowed to store a copy
Each layer may cache a copy of the response as it passes through, for future requests
The response is deleted at the edge layer to save storage
Only the origin retains any copy of the response
items.explanation: As a fresh response travels back, each layer it passes through can cache it, so a later request for the same thing might be answered from any of those layers instead of all the way from the origin.

items.prompt: Why is it misleading to think of caching as just "CDN or no CDN"?
choices: Because CDNs are actually unrelated to caching entirely
Because caching happens at multiple layers (browser, edge, and effectively the origin's own cache if it has one) — a CDN is one layer among several
Because only origins can cache content, not CDNs
Because browsers never actually cache anything
items.explanation: Caching exists at more than one layer between a browser and an origin — treating it as a single binary switch misses that each layer can independently hit or miss.

items.prompt: A request for a popular image hits the visitor's browser cache (miss, first time on this device) and then the CDN edge cache (hit, another visitor near this PoP recently loaded it). Where does this particular request end up being answered from?
choices: The origin server, since the browser missed
The CDN edge cache — the origin is never reached for this request
Both the edge cache and the origin, to double-check
It fails, since a browser miss always requires an origin trip
items.explanation: A browser-cache miss only escalates to the next layer, the CDN edge — which has it, so the response is served from there; the origin is never involved in answering this particular request.

Where else have you seen a system escalate through layers only when the cheaper ones fail?

items.prompt: Two visitors, one in Tokyo and one in São Paulo, request the exact same uncached static image for the first time ever, globally. What does each visitor's edge server have to do, and what does that briefly mean for the origin?
choices: Neither edge server needs to contact the origin, since the content is static
Each edge server independently misses and has to fetch from the origin — so the origin may see more than one request for the same content before both edges have cached it
Only one of the two edge servers is allowed to contact the origin at a time
The two edge servers directly share their caches with each other, bypassing the origin entirely
items.explanation: Each geographically separate edge cache starts empty for content it has never seen — so the very first requests from different regions can each independently miss and reach the origin, before the content is cached at each of those edges.

The origin would see dramatically more traffic than if browser caching were also disabled
CDN edge caching becomes entirely non-functional without browser caching enabled
items.explanation: Skipping browser caching means even a returning visitor's unchanged assets have to be re-requested over the network every time, even though the CDN layer still protects the origin from most of that traffic.

The request is forced all the way to the origin regardless of what the edge has
The browser and the CDN edge must always agree on freshness, so this situation cannot occur
items.explanation: A stale copy at one layer simply means that layer can't answer anymore — it escalates to the next layer, which independently checks its own freshness and can answer from there without needing the origin at all.

items.prompt: What is a "cache hit"?
choices: A request that fails to find any cached copy anywhere
A request answered immediately from a cached copy already at that layer, with no trip further upstream
A request that corrupts the cache on arrival
A request that always bypasses TTL checks
items.explanation: A cache hit means the layer already had a fresh, usable copy and could answer immediately, without asking the next layer up.

items.prompt: What is a "cache miss"?
choices: A request that the server rejects outright
A request where that layer doesn't have a fresh copy, so it has to ask the next layer up
A request that always triggers a cache purge
A request that only happens on the very first visit to a site, ever
items.explanation: A miss means the layer being checked doesn't have a fresh copy, so the request escalates to the next layer — and whatever comes back may get cached there for next time.

items.prompt: What does TTL ("time to live") control?
choices: How many visitors are allowed to access a cached copy
How long a cached copy is trusted as fresh before it must be re-validated or re-fetched
How much disk space a cache is allowed to use
How quickly a request travels across the network
items.explanation: TTL is a duration: how long a cache is allowed to treat a stored copy as still good, before treating it as stale and going back to the origin.

items.prompt: What's the trade-off of choosing a very short TTL?
choices: Fresher content, but more trips back to the origin
Fresher content, with no extra cost at all
Staler content, but fewer origin trips
No trade-off — TTL length has no real effect on anything
items.explanation: A short TTL means cached copies expire quickly, so content stays fresher, but at the cost of more frequent trips back to the origin to refresh them.

items.prompt: What's the trade-off of choosing a very long TTL?
choices: Fresher content and fewer origin trips, with no downside
Fewer origin trips, but a higher chance of serving something that's gone stale
More origin trips, but guaranteed freshness
Long TTLs are simply not allowed by the HTTP spec
items.explanation: A long TTL reduces how often the origin gets asked, but it also increases the window during which a cached copy might be outdated relative to the real, current data.

items.prompt: If a cache layer's hit ratio goes from 0% to 90%, what happens to the number of requests the origin actually has to answer?
choices: It stays exactly the same — hit ratio only affects speed, not origin load
It drops dramatically, since the origin only sees the requests every other layer couldn't answer
It increases, since caching adds overhead for the origin to track
It becomes impossible to measure
items.explanation: A 90% hit ratio means 90% of requests are answered without reaching the origin — the origin's workload drops roughly in proportion to the miss rate, not the hit rate.

items.prompt: Does a high cache hit ratio mean "everything got about 10x faster on average," or something more specific?
choices: Yes, that's exactly and only what it means
It specifically means the origin — the hardest layer to scale — sees dramatically less traffic, not just "things feel faster"
It means the origin has become entirely unnecessary
It means every individual request is now guaranteed to be a hit
items.explanation: The unit is specific: a high hit ratio means the origin itself sees far less traffic, which matters because the origin is usually the single hardest part of the system to scale — it's a load-reduction effect, not just an average-speed effect.

items.prompt: Is every piece of content equally safe to cache for the same length of time?
choices: Yes, TTL should always be identical across all content on a site
No — something like a blog post's HTML might be fine to cache for minutes, while a logged-in user's account balance usually shouldn't be cached for anyone but that user, if at all
No, but only images and videos ever need special treatment
Yes, as long as the CDN vendor is reputable
items.explanation: Cacheability and appropriate TTL depend on the content — fairly static, shared content tolerates caching well, while personalized or rapidly-changing data often shouldn't be cached the same way, or at all.

items.prompt: A news homepage sets a 30-second TTL on its content. What is this choosing, and why might that be the right call for that specific content?
choices: Choosing maximum freshness with zero cost — there's no trade-off involved
Accepting a bounded, short window of possible staleness in exchange for not hammering the origin on every single request
Guaranteeing that the content is always 100% up to date at every moment
Preventing the content from ever being cached at any layer
items.explanation: A 30-second TTL accepts that visitors might see content up to 30 seconds old, in exchange for not sending every single request straight to the origin — a reasonable trade for content that changes often but not instantly.

Long TTL

Why: TTL length is a dial between freshness and origin load, not a setting with one universally correct value.

Where have you seen a system choose between "ask more often, stay fresher" and "ask less often, risk staleness"?

items.prompt: A cache hit ratio improves from 50% to 99% after a TTL change. Which statement most precisely describes the effect on the origin?

The origin now handles roughly 1/50th as many requests as before, since it only sees the share of requests that miss
The origin sees no change, since hit ratio only affects visitor-perceived speed
The origin's load becomes completely unpredictable
items.explanation: At 50% hits, the origin sees 50% of requests (the misses). At 99% hits, it sees only 1% — a roughly 50x reduction in origin-facing traffic, not just a "somewhat less" change.

items.prompt: A system has a cache hit ratio of 0%. What does that tell you about TTL or caching configuration?

items.prompt: Who decides what gets cached and for how long, according to the unit?
choices: Each cache layer decides independently, with no coordination
The origin server, via instructions in HTTP response headers like Cache-Control
The visitor's browser settings alone
DNS servers, as part of resolving the hostname
items.explanation: The origin sets the rules via response headers; every cache along the way follows those instructions rather than guessing independently.

items.prompt: What does the `public` directive on Cache-Control tell caches?
choices: Only the requesting browser may store this response
Any cache — browser, CDN, shared proxy — may store this response
The response must never be cached anywhere
The response is visible to anyone on the internet, regardless of auth
items.explanation: `public` means the response is safe for any cache, including shared ones like a CDN, to store — not just the one browser that requested it.

items.prompt: What does the `private` directive on Cache-Control tell caches?
choices: Any shared cache, like a CDN, may store it for all visitors
Only the requesting browser's own cache may store it — a CDN or other shared cache must not
The response must be encrypted before caching
It has no real effect on caching behavior
items.explanation: `private` restricts caching to the one browser that made the request — a CDN or any other shared cache is not permitted to store it for reuse by other visitors.

Browsers treat fingerprinted files as a special protocol
items.explanation: Because the filename changes whenever the content changes, the old filename's content is permanently frozen — there's no staleness risk to protect against, so an aggressive, long cache is safe.

Change the filename itself whenever content changes, so the cache never needs to expire the old (now-irrelevant) URL
Manually purge every CDN edge node after each deploy
Disable caching for static assets entirely
items.explanation: Instead of expiring a cache entry, a new version gets a new filename — the old filename's cached content becomes irrelevant rather than needing active invalidation.

items.prompt: Why does a plain, non-fingerprinted `/favicon.ico` need a real TTL instead of caching forever?

Browsers refuse to cache any file without a fingerprinted name

Force every visitor to wait for a fresh origin fetch on every single request
Serve a random mix of a stale and fresh copy, alternating by visitor
items.explanation: It serves the (slightly outdated) cached copy right away, with no visitor waiting on the origin, while one background fetch quietly updates the cache for whoever asks next.

items.prompt: Why should a shopping cart or account dashboard generally not be cached at any shared layer?

items.explanation: The risk with personalized, dynamic content isn't just staleness — a shared cache serving the same stored response to multiple visitors would leak one person's private data to someone else.

items.prompt: Which of these would most likely be cached the most aggressively (longest effective freshness)?

items.prompt: Does "dynamic content" automatically mean "cannot be cached"?

Yes, but only for content generated by a database
No, dynamic content is always cached the same way as static content

items.prompt: What is the "cache invalidation problem"?
choices: Deciding how big a cache's storage should be
The challenge that a cached copy has no way of knowing the origin's data changed, unless something tells it
A bug that only affects browser caches, never CDNs
The process of deleting all caches simultaneously on a schedule
items.explanation: A CDN edge server has no inherent way to detect that the origin's underlying data changed — invalidation is about how (or whether) it finds out before the TTL naturally expires.

items.prompt: What is the "wait it out" invalidation strategy?
choices: Immediately notify every edge server the moment data changes
Set a short enough TTL that staleness is bounded and acceptable, without any active invalidation step
Refuse to cache any content that might ever change
Manually refresh every cache entry once per day regardless of changes
items.explanation: Waiting it out means relying purely on a short TTL to bound how long content can be stale — simple, but every visitor within that window might see the old version.

items.prompt: What is "purge on demand"?
choices: Automatically purging the entire cache every hour on a timer
The origin explicitly telling the CDN "this URL is now stale, drop it" the moment the underlying data changes
A visitor manually clearing their own browser cache
Disabling caching permanently for a given URL
items.explanation: Purge on demand is an active notification: the origin tells caches exactly when and what changed, rather than waiting for a TTL to naturally expire.

items.prompt: What's the main cost of the "wait it out" (short TTL) approach?
choices: It requires the origin to track exactly what changed
More frequent trips back to the origin to re-fetch content
It guarantees immediate freshness with no staleness window at all
It cannot be used for any kind of content
items.explanation: A short TTL bounds staleness but means caches re-check with the origin far more often, increasing origin load compared to a longer TTL.

items.prompt: What's the main cost of "purge on demand"?
choices: It cannot guarantee freshness at all
The origin has to know exactly what to invalidate and tell every edge server, worldwide, in time — added complexity
It always increases origin load compared to a short TTL
It only works for static assets, never for dynamic pages
items.explanation: Purge-based invalidation trades simplicity for freshness: it requires tracking exactly what changed and propagating that purge everywhere it's cached, which is real added complexity.

items.prompt: According to the comparison table, which strategy has lower origin load: short TTL, or long TTL + purge?
choices: Short TTL has lower origin load
Long TTL + purge has lower origin load, since re-fetches are rare outside of explicit purges
They have identical origin load in all cases
Origin load is unrelated to either strategy
items.explanation: A long TTL means the origin is asked rarely (only on purges or natural expiry), while a short TTL means frequent re-fetches regardless of whether anything actually changed.

items.prompt: Why is cache invalidation described as one of the hard problems in computer science?
choices: Because it requires exotic, rarely-used hardware
Because a cached copy fundamentally has no built-in way to know the source data changed — someone has to design a mechanism for that, and every mechanism has trade-offs
Because it's only relevant to CDNs and no other kind of system
Because there's a single correct universal solution nobody has implemented yet
items.explanation: The difficulty isn't technical obscurity — it's that there's no free way for a cached copy to "just know" the source changed; every solution (short TTL, purge, etc.) involves a genuine trade-off.

items.prompt: An admin edits a published article immediately after publishing a typo fix. Which strategy gets the fix visible to all visitors the fastest?
choices: Waiting for a long TTL to naturally expire
Purge on demand — explicitly invalidating the cached copy the moment the edit happens
Neither strategy can ever update content faster than the original TTL
Shortening the TTL after the fact, retroactively
items.explanation: Purge on demand directly tells caches to drop the stale copy right when the change happens, rather than waiting for any TTL window to pass.

items.prompt: A team relies purely on a 24-hour TTL for a page that occasionally needs urgent corrections (e.g. a factual error). What's the practical consequence of not having a purge mechanism?
choices: No consequence — a 24-hour TTL is always short enough for any use case
An urgent correction could remain invisible to some visitors for up to 24 hours, until the TTL naturally expires
The origin would be overloaded by constant re-fetching
The content becomes permanently stuck in its stale state forever
items.explanation: Without an active invalidation path, the only way stale content gets refreshed is the TTL expiring — for urgent corrections, that bounded wait can still be an uncomfortably long window.

items.prompt: What problem does "origin shielding" solve?
choices: It encrypts traffic between the CDN and the origin
Without it, every one of hundreds of edge PoPs could independently ask the origin on a miss, multiplying load; shielding routes misses through one designated location first
It prevents any cache misses from ever occurring
It replaces the need for Cache-Control headers entirely
items.explanation: Origin shielding funnels cache misses through one shield location, so the origin sees at most one request per miss instead of one per PoP per miss.

items.prompt: Without origin shielding, what could happen when a popular piece of content expires simultaneously at many edge PoPs?
choices: Nothing changes — only one PoP is ever allowed to ask the origin
Each PoP could independently ask the origin at roughly the same time, multiplying the load the origin actually sees
The content would be permanently deleted from all PoPs
The origin would automatically shield itself with no configuration needed
items.explanation: Each edge PoP operates somewhat independently — without shielding, many PoPs missing around the same time can each separately hit the origin, amplifying load rather than reducing it.

items.prompt: What is a "cache key," in CDN terms?
choices: A secret password required to access cached content
What the CDN considers "the same request" for caching purposes — by default, usually the URL
An encryption key used to scramble cached response bodies
A unique ID assigned to each individual visitor
items.explanation: The cache key defines what counts as an identical request for caching purposes — by default just the URL, but it can be widened or narrowed.

items.prompt: What happens if a cache key is defined too narrowly (doesn't include something that should distinguish requests)?
choices: Caching becomes impossible entirely
Different content can collide under one cached response, serving the wrong content to the wrong visitor
The CDN automatically falls back to never caching
Nothing — narrow cache keys have no real downside
items.explanation: A too-narrow key causes requests that should get different responses to share one cached entry — a classic cause of serving user A's content to user B.

items.prompt: What happens if a cache key is defined too broadly (includes things that don't actually change the response)?
choices: It guarantees the correct response is always served
The same content gets needlessly duplicated across many cache keys, crushing the hit ratio
It has no measurable effect on caching efficiency
It automatically narrows itself over time
items.explanation: A too-broad key splits what should be one cached entry into many near-identical ones (e.g. varying by something irrelevant), so each gets fewer hits and the overall hit ratio suffers.

items.prompt: Can a cache key be widened to include something other than just the URL?
choices: No, a cache key is always exactly the URL with no exceptions
Yes — it can be widened to include a header, a cookie, or a query parameter
Yes, but only by changing the URL structure itself
No, cache keys are fixed by the HTTP specification
items.explanation: A cache key's scope is configurable — it can be widened to factor in things like a header, cookie, or query parameter when the response genuinely varies by those.

items.prompt: Roughly what does the origin's real workload look like, after a CDN with shielding and a well-designed cache key is in front of it?

Zero requests, ever, once a CDN is configured
Exactly the same volume, just delayed by network latency

items.prompt: Stripped of vendor-specific UI, what is an edge cache fundamentally doing?
choices: Encrypting every request before forwarding it to the origin
Acting as a key-value store in front of an origin fetch, where the key is derived from the request and the value carries a body plus its own expiry
Permanently replicating the origin's entire database at every PoP
Randomly deciding whether to forward each request to the origin
items.explanation: At its core, an edge cache is just a lookup: derive a key from the request, check if a stored value is still fresh, and only fall through to the origin on a miss.

items.prompt: In the minimal edge cache's logic, what happens on a cache hit (a stored entry whose age is still under its maxAge)?
choices: The origin is still contacted anyway, just to confirm
The stored response is returned immediately, marked as a HIT, with no origin fetch
The entry is deleted immediately after being read
The response is returned, but marked as a MISS by mistake
items.explanation: A hit means the cached entry is still within its freshness window — it's returned directly, with no need to reach the origin at all.

items.prompt: What decides whether a fresh response from the origin actually gets stored in the cache?
choices: Every response is stored automatically, with no conditions
Whether the origin's own response headers (like Cache-Control: public with a max-age) say the response is storable
Whether the edge server has spare disk space at that exact moment
Whether the request method was GET specifically, regardless of headers
items.explanation: The cache checks the origin's own Cache-Control signal — if it isn't explicitly public with a usable max-age, the cache does not store it, mirroring L2's "the origin decides" rule.

items.prompt: If an origin response has no Cache-Control header at all, what should a well-behaved edge cache do by default?
choices: Cache it forever, since no header means no restriction
Treat it as not cacheable — don't store it — rather than assuming it's safe to cache
Ask the visitor's browser what to do instead
Cache it for exactly 60 seconds as a universal default
items.explanation: Silence from the origin should be treated as "don't cache this," not "cache it indefinitely" — caching something the origin never explicitly opted into is the more dangerous mistake.

items.prompt: What is a "cache key" built from, in a minimal edge cache implementation?
choices: Only the visitor's IP address
The request method and URL, plus optionally any headers/values the response is known to vary by (varyOn)
A random number generated per request
The exact timestamp the request arrived
items.explanation: A cache key typically combines method + URL, optionally extended with specific headers or cookie values the response varies by — exactly the configurable "cache key" concept introduced in L2.

items.prompt: What does "purge" do to a minimal edge cache's internal store?
choices: It doubles the maxAge of the targeted entry
It removes the stored entry for a specific cache key, forcing the next request for it to be treated as a miss
It deletes every entry in the entire cache, regardless of key
It converts the entry from public to private
items.explanation: A purge targets one specific cache key and removes just that entry — the next matching request has to go to the origin again, since there's nothing cached under that key anymore.

items.prompt: Why is a minimal edge cache like this one, with "no clustering, no multi-region replication, no LRU eviction," still a useful thing to study?
choices: It isn't useful — real CDNs work completely differently under the hood
Every real CDN's edge logic is a more sophisticated version of exactly the same core steps: derive a key, check freshness, fetch on miss, store per the origin's instructions
It's only useful for understanding browser caches, not CDN edge caches
Minimal implementations are purely academic and never resemble production systems
items.explanation: The mechanism scales up (clustering, replication, eviction policies) in real systems, but the fundamental steps — key, freshness check, miss-then-fetch, conditional store — stay the same.

items.prompt: What's the key difference between a cache "MISS" and a cache "STALE" result in this model?
choices: There is no difference — they're two names for the same thing
A MISS means there was no prior entry at all; a STALE result means there was a prior entry, but it had expired, so the origin was asked again
STALE means the response is corrupted and unusable
MISS only happens on the very first request ever made to the whole cache
items.explanation: A MISS is a cold lookup with nothing stored yet; a STALE result still reflects an expired prior entry being refreshed — both result in an origin fetch, but they describe different starting states.

items.prompt: Using the minimal edge cache's logic, if `fetchFromOrigin` returns headers with no `Cache-Control` header at all, what happens to that response?
choices: It's stored anyway, since an absent header is treated as permissive by default
It's returned to the caller, but never stored — the cache is left exactly as it was before the request
The request fails outright with an error
It's stored, but only for exactly 60 seconds
items.explanation: An empty/absent Cache-Control means the "is this public with a usable max-age" check fails, so the store step is skipped entirely — the response still reaches the caller, it just isn't cached for next time.

items.prompt: In the leaked-greeting example, what was the root cause of Bob receiving a response meant for Alice?
choices: The origin sent the wrong data to the CDN directly
The cache key was built from the URL alone, ignoring the session cookie that actually determined the response content
Bob's browser had a corrupted cache
The CDN randomly serves cached responses to the wrong visitor sometimes
items.explanation: The cache key didn't include anything that distinguished Alice's session from Bob's — so once Alice's request populated the cache under that key, any later request to the same URL (including Bob's) got her stored response back.

items.prompt: Why did the cached response get reused for Bob's request even though his session cookie was completely different from Alice's?
choices: Because cookies are ignored by all CDNs as a matter of policy
Because the cache key that determines "is this the same request" never looked at the cookie at all
Because Bob's request happened to also use the session value sess-alice
Because the cache had already expired by the time Bob made his request
items.explanation: The cache only checks whatever is part of the key — since the cookie wasn't part of it, the cache had no way to tell Alice's and Bob's requests apart, even though the actual response content depended on that cookie.

items.prompt: What are the two general fixes to this specific kind of leak, according to the unit?
choices: Encrypt the response body, or reduce the TTL to zero
Include the identifying header/cookie in the cache key (varyOn), or mark the response private/no-store so a shared cache never stores it at all
Delete the user's session after every single request
Switch to a different CDN vendor entirely
items.explanation: Either widen the cache key to actually distinguish requests that get different content, or opt the response out of shared caching entirely — those are the two real fixes described.

items.prompt: Why does the unit note that including the cookie in varyOn "usually defeats the purpose of caching a personalized response at all"?
choices: Because varyOn is a deprecated feature that no longer works
Because if the key now includes a per-user identifier, each user effectively gets their own private cache entry — there's no sharing benefit left, since no two users' keys would ever match
Because varyOn always disables storage outright
Because cookies cannot technically be read by cache logic
items.explanation: Once the key is unique per user, the cache stops being "shared" in any meaningful sense — you're caching one response per user, which is rarely worth the overhead for something this personalized.

items.prompt: What is the more common, practical fix for a personalized endpoint like `/api/me`, per the unit?
choices: Add every possible header to the cache key just in case
Mark the response `private` or `no-store` so a shared CDN cache never stores it in the first place
Cache it anyway, but reduce the TTL to a few seconds
Serve it exclusively over a different, unrelated domain
items.explanation: Rather than widening the key to uniqueness (which defeats shared caching anyway), the more common fix is simply opting the response out of shared caching entirely with private/no-store, consistent with L2's guidance.

items.prompt: In the fixed version of the example, what Cache-Control value is used for the personalized greeting response?

private, no-store
public, immutable

items.explanation: The fixed handler marks the response `private, no-store`, explicitly telling any shared cache not to store it, so it can never be replayed to a different user.

items.prompt: What is a "cache stampede" (thundering herd)?
choices: A gradual, steady increase in cache misses over several hours
A cached entry expiring while hundreds or thousands of near-simultaneous requests all miss at once and all hit the origin together
A deliberate attack that floods a cache with fake entries
The normal, expected behavior of any cache with a short TTL
items.explanation: It's specifically about simultaneity: many concurrent requests discovering a miss at the same instant and independently forwarding to the origin all at once, briefly reproducing the exact overload a CDN exists to prevent.

items.prompt: Why does a naive edge cache implementation make a stampede worse, not better?
choices: It doesn't — naive implementations are immune to stampedes
Every concurrent miss independently calls the origin fetch, so N simultaneous requests for the same expired key become N separate origin calls
It refuses all requests during a miss, causing errors instead of a stampede
It always serves stale data forever, preventing any origin calls
items.explanation: A naive cache has no mechanism to notice that many requests are asking for the same thing at once — it just repeats the same fetch logic independently for each one, multiplying origin load exactly when the origin is least prepared for it.

items.prompt: What does "request coalescing" do?
choices: It merges multiple different URLs into a single cached entry
The first miss for a key triggers the origin fetch; every other concurrent request for that same key waits on the in-flight fetch instead of starting a new one
It deletes duplicate requests before they reach the cache at all
It increases the TTL automatically whenever a stampede is detected
items.explanation: Coalescing collapses many concurrent requests for the same key into exactly one origin fetch — everyone else just waits for and shares that single result.

items.prompt: How does `stale-while-revalidate` prevent a stampede differently from request coalescing?
choices: It also waits on one shared in-flight fetch, just with a different name
It serves the existing (now slightly stale) cached copy immediately to every request, while exactly one background fetch refreshes the cache for later requests
It rejects all requests until the refresh completes
It deletes the stale entry immediately so no one can read it
items.explanation: Unlike coalescing (which still makes requests wait on a fetch), stale-while-revalidate never makes anyone wait — it answers instantly from the stale copy while one quiet background fetch catches the cache up.

items.prompt: With stale-while-revalidate, do visitors ever experience a delay waiting for the origin during a stampede event?
choices: Yes, every visitor waits for the full origin round trip
No — visitors get the existing cached copy immediately; only one background fetch talks to the origin, invisibly to everyone
Only the very first visitor experiences a delay
It depends on which specific CDN vendor is used
items.explanation: The whole point of SWR is that visitor-facing latency stays flat — nobody waits on the origin, they just occasionally get a response that's a few seconds older than the absolute latest.

items.prompt: Which kind of page would a cache stampede be most dangerous for: a static marketing page, or an origin that also handles checkout writes?
choices: Equally dangerous for both, with no meaningful difference
The origin handling checkout writes — the same stampede there risks taking down purchasing entirely, not just causing a performance blip
The static marketing page, since it has no database behind it at all
Neither is actually at risk from a stampede
items.explanation: The mechanism (many simultaneous misses hitting the origin) is identical, but the consequences scale with what the origin is also responsible for — overloading an origin that also processes payments is a much bigger deal than a brief slowdown on a read-only marketing page.

items.prompt: In the coalescing implementation shown, what does `inFlight.get(key)` returning an existing promise mean?
choices: That key has never been requested before
A fetch for that exact key is already in progress — this request should just wait on (reuse) that same promise instead of starting a new fetch
The cache has permanently failed for that key
The key has expired and needs an immediate purge
items.explanation: If an entry already exists in the in-flight map for that key, it means another request got there first and already kicked off the origin fetch — this new request rides along on that same result rather than duplicating the work.

items.prompt: After the in-flight fetch for a key resolves (or fails), what does `.finally(() => this.inFlight.delete(key))` ensure?
choices: That the key is cached forever once resolved
That the in-flight tracking entry is cleaned up, so the next genuinely new request for that key (after this one completes) starts a fresh fetch rather than waiting on a stale promise
That the fetch is automatically retried three times
That the cache key itself is deleted along with the tracking entry
items.explanation: Cleanup matters: once the shared fetch finishes, the in-flight marker needs to be removed so future requests (after this round) don't mistakenly wait on an already-completed promise instead of fetching fresh data when it's actually needed again.

items.prompt: A popular page's cache entry expires, and 2,000 requests arrive within the same 50ms window. With request coalescing in place, how many actual fetches reach the origin?
choices: 2,000 — coalescing doesn't reduce the number of origin fetches

0 — coalescing blocks all requests until the TTL resets
It depends on the exact CDN vendor's internal configuration
items.explanation: Coalescing collapses all concurrent requests for the same key into exactly one real origin fetch — everyone else waits on and shares that single in-flight promise rather than starting their own.

items.prompt: What is a "purge race"?
choices: A competition between two CDN vendors over purge speed
The gap between an origin's purge request going out and every globally distributed edge PoP actually receiving and applying it
A bug where purges happen too frequently, overloading the origin
The normal, expected delay before a TTL expires
items.explanation: A purge race is about propagation timing: purges to hundreds of distributed PoPs aren't instantaneous or atomic, so a request can land at a PoP that hasn't received the purge yet.

items.prompt: During the purge propagation window, what might a request hitting a not-yet-updated PoP receive?
choices: An automatic error page explaining the purge is in progress
The old, now-incorrect cached content, for however long propagation takes at that PoP
A redirect to a different, already-updated PoP
Nothing — such a PoP would simply refuse to answer at all
items.explanation: A PoP that hasn't yet received the purge still has the old entry and will serve it as if it were still valid, since from that PoP's perspective nothing has changed yet.

items.prompt: Is purge propagation delay considered a bug to be fixed, or a real trade-off, according to the unit?
choices: A simple bug that any competent engineering team can eliminate entirely
A real trade-off inherent to running caches on machines physically distributed worldwide, communicating over a real network with real latency
Not a real concern in practice, since purges are always instant
A problem that only affects CDNs with fewer than 10 PoPs
items.explanation: The unit frames this explicitly as a property of physical distribution and network latency, not a fixable implementation bug — propagation delay is structural, even if it's often very fast.

items.prompt: What does the `purgeAndVerify` pattern actually do?
choices: It purges a URL once and immediately assumes success with no further checking
It purges, then repeatedly re-fetches the URL (bypassing cache) and checks whether the returned version matches what's expected, retrying with backoff until it does or attempts run out
It permanently disables caching for that URL after the first purge
It verifies the purge by checking server logs instead of making real requests
items.explanation: It's a defensive polling pattern: purge, then actively confirm (via a no-cache fetch) that the new version is actually being served, retrying with increasing delays if it isn't yet.

items.prompt: Why does `purgeAndVerify` use increasing delays between retry attempts (`200 * (attempt + 1)`) instead of a fixed delay?
choices: It's purely an arbitrary stylistic choice with no functional reason
It gives propagation progressively more time to catch up on each retry, rather than hammering the same not-yet-updated endpoint at a fixed, possibly too-short interval
A fixed delay would be illegal under HTTP's specification
It has no effect at all on the retry behavior
items.explanation: Increasing the wait between attempts gives more time for propagation to actually complete as retries continue, rather than repeatedly checking too soon with no benefit.

items.prompt: Which category of content does the unit suggest might need a different mechanism entirely, rather than relying on cache purge?
choices: A blog post with a typo fix
Something that truly cannot tolerate any propagation window at all — an emergency takedown or a leaked-secret redaction
A product listing page's price update
A static image asset's filename change
items.explanation: For genuinely zero-tolerance cases (an emergency takedown, a leaked secret), the unit suggests routing that URL through an "always ask origin" rule until the purge is confirmed everywhere, rather than trusting purge propagation timing at all.

items.prompt: What determines whether a purge race matters a little or a lot, according to the unit's closing framing?
choices: It's always equally serious, regardless of what content is involved

Only the geographic distance between PoPs matters, not the content
Purge races only matter for video content specifically
items.explanation: The unit explicitly contrasts stakes: the exact same technical race condition is low-stakes for some content and a real incident for other content, depending on what's being served.

items.prompt: Why can't a purge simply be made instantaneous and atomic across every PoP worldwide, in principle?
choices: It actually can be made instantaneous with the right software, and vendors just haven't bothered
Because PoPs are physically distributed machines communicating over a real network — any communication across real distance and real infrastructure takes some non-zero time
Because purges are processed by a human operator at each PoP manually
Because atomicity is prevented by a deliberate design choice with no underlying reason
items.explanation: This is a physical/structural constraint, not a design oversight: coordinating state across many physically separate machines over a real network cannot be instantaneous, even if it's often very fast in practice.

items.prompt: An admin purges a paywalled article moments after fixing an incorrect price. A request lands at a PoP that hasn't received the purge yet, 300ms later. What does that visitor see?
choices: The newly corrected price, since the purge was already issued
The old, incorrect price — that specific PoP hasn't applied the purge yet and is still serving its stale cached copy
An error page, since the content is mid-purge
A blank page until propagation completes everywhere
items.explanation: A purge being issued doesn't mean every PoP has it yet — a PoP that hasn't received the purge continues serving its existing (now stale) cached entry exactly as if nothing had changed.
